extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film students, critics, and researchers interested in mockumentary filmmaking and the 2002 film Opération Lune / Dark Side of the Moon
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria relevant to making or evaluating a mockumentary that stages a historical hoax: elements to use (real interviews, actors, archival footage), how to signal parody, and precautions to avoid genuinely deceiving audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conspiracist tonality
rubrics_metrics.description: Karel took care to avoid any conspiracist tonality; in particular, at no point is it said that Armstrong did not walk on the Moon. The script hypothesizes that the US might have wanted a contingency plan if the first steps could not be filmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the premise as a hypothetical contingency or satirical what-if rather than asserting false claims. This reduces risk of promoting actual conspiracy belief while enabling parody.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple element types to construct plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The film uses four main types of elements: interviews (real and staged), recycled archival footage, actors playing witnesses, and deceptive subtitling in parts of the film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine authentic-seeming materials (real interview snippets, archival clips) with staged components to craft a convincing narrative; be deliberate about which element serves which narrative purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview technique: deceptive pretext and vague questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Karel interviewed Kubrick's widow, Jan Harlan, Vernon Walters, Buzz Aldrin and others pretending to make a bona fide documentary and asking intentionally vague questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vague or leading questions to elicit lines that can be recontextualized in editing. Note ethical and legal considerations when interviewing under a false pretext.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recycle and edit archival footage to twist meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Footage of Nixon staff and others was recycled from earlier documentaries and edited in order to twist their words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selective editing of archival material can create new implications, but carries ethical risks and can be later mistaken for factual reporting; consider disclaimers or giveaway devices to reduce harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage actors as 'witnesses' to bridge narrative gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Other 'witnesses' are played by actors to make the connections between the sentences pronounced by 'real witnesses' and make a credible story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interleave actors with real interviewees to manufacture continuity; choose actor roles and names that serve both the story and, if desired, act as subtle giveaways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fictitious character names as intentional giveaways
rubrics_metrics.description: Many fictitious witnesses are named after characters in Kubrick and Hitchcock films (e.g., Jack Torrance, David Bowman, Eve Kendall) and are listed in credits along with the actors portraying them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embedding meta-references (character names drawn from films) is an explicit signal to alert informed viewers that the film is fictional or satirical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce factual errors and anachronisms as giveaways
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator deliberately inserts factual errors (e.g., JFK speech year wrong, Luna 9 landing month wrong, incorrect Apollo 11 launch date, misstatements about Korolev, mislabeling Johnson and Nixon as governors, incorrect Bush family connection, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planting verifiable mistakes and anachronisms provides viewers with checkable clues that the piece is not a straightforward documentary; list of concrete examples appears in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include parodic bloopers/end-credits to make hoax obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodic bloopers are added in the end credits showing participants laughing or failing to remember lines, so that if viewers still believed the hoax they would be disabused by the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overtly parodic end-credit material to convert any remaining ambiguity into clear satire; this functions as a fail-safe to limit genuine deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize visible special effects to preserve documentary feel
rubrics_metrics.description: Only one image (a portrait of Kubrick on lunar soil) uses a special effect—otherwise the film avoids obvious special effects to maintain verisimilitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrained use of effects helps the fiction feel documentary-real; sparing effects plus archival footage increase perceived authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accompany broadcast with contextual materials (web quiz, debate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arte accompanied the airing with a website featuring a quiz and ran a debate; the web quiz led players to guess in which films characters' names originally appeared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide external contextualization (website, post-screening debate, quizzes) to guide interpretation and reveal the spoof’s mechanisms to audiences who might otherwise be misled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subjects that are historical and universal but not overly sensitive
rubrics_metrics.description: The filmmakers sought a topic that would be universal and historical but not sensitive like a war; hence the Moon landing was chosen as suitable material for parody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting a subject less likely to inflame genuine hurt or political backlash reduces ethical risk while retaining broad recognizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use juxtaposition/editing to create layered 'hoax within a hoax'
rubrics_metrics.description: The closing bloopers create a 'hoax within a hoax'—showing real characters joking can give the false impression they voluntarily participated in the hoax, and some apparently joking lines were actually serious in earlier documentaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that meta-editing tricks can backfire and create additional ambiguity about participants' intentions; document provenance of reused footage to avoid misattribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate ethical/misuse risks: audiences may take satire as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When shown to students studying conspiracy theories, many believed the film was sincere; conspiracy advocates later cited the film as evidence for their views and extracts were reposted online as 'proof'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for potential misuse: include clear giveaways, contextual materials, and public explanation to reduce the chance that satirical work will be appropriated by conspiracy movements.
